summary: CDAS introduces a genuinely novel perspective on intervention-based steering by combining a JSD distribution-matching objective with Distributed Interchange Interventions (DII) inspired by DAS, framing steering as causal concept-feature identification rather than fine-tuning. The two safety case studies (refusal override and CoT backdoor neutralization) are practically relevant and the faithfulness analysis via KL divergence is a useful contribution. However, the central thesis—that implicit factor sampling yields 'faithful, tuning-free' steering—is contradicted by the paper's own results: the principled 'unit factor' configuration fails badly on AXBENCH (scores 0.12–0.24) and CDAS only becomes competitive with inference-time factor tuning via grid search, the very practice it argues against. Combined with absent error bars in all main tables, a single 2B-vs-9B comparison underlying the scale claim, and cherry-picked baselines, the evidence does not yet support the paper's claims at an ICLR acceptance bar.
strengths: Novel conceptual framing of steering as causal concept-feature identification via DII/DAS inspiration rather than parameter-efficient fine-tuning, connecting steering to mechanistic interpretability.

The JSD-based distribution-matching objective is a well-motivated alternative to Lang./PO objectives, using the model's own counterfactual distribution as teacher signal, and is a genuine methodological contribution.

The two safety case studies target practically important problems (refusal override for quality-of-service; backdoor neutralization) and the faithfulness evaluation via KL divergence and standard-benchmark preservation is meaningful beyond steering effectiveness alone.

The paper is commendably honest about limitations in the conclusion (stricter data requirements, need for factor tuning, rank-1 only, lack of rigorous causal grounding), which is good scientific practice.
Bi-directional steering emerges naturally from the DII protocol without requiring separate objectives for elicitation vs. suppression, an elegant design property.

key_concerns.issue: The central narrative—that CDAS provides 'faithful' steering by implicitly sampling factors from the model's natural distribution, avoiding 'off-distribution' tuned factors—is directly contradicted by Table 1: unit-factor scores are 0.121/0.127/0.238/0.120, far below tuned-factor (0.631/0.608/0.992/0.518) and below all competitors. The paper itself states 'factor tuning is paramount for CDAS.' If the principled, tuning-free version does not work, the 'faithful' framing in the title and abstract is unsupported, and CDAS-with-tuning is not clearly better than RePS-with-tuning.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Either (a) diagnose and fix why unit-factor fails so the principled configuration is competitive, or (b) reframe the contribution honestly: drop 'faithful' from the title, position tuned-factor CDAS as a complement to RePS, and base claims only on the configuration actually used. A method whose principled form underperforms cannot claim faithfulness as its headline property.

key_concerns.issue: Statistical rigor is insufficient for the claims made. Tables 1–4 report single numbers with no error bars, no variance, and no significance tests. The 'consistency across layers' claim (0.023 change for CDAS vs. 0.150 for RePS on Gemma-2-2B) is based on single runs and is not statistically meaningful. Figure 1 uses only 3 random initializations. It is impossible to judge whether CDAS's apparent advantages are real or noise.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Report all main-table results over multiple seeds (≥5) with mean ± std and, where comparisons are made, paired significance tests. Re-examine whether the 'consistency' and 'scale benefit' claims survive once variance is accounted for.

key_concerns.issue: The 'CDAS benefits from model scale' claim is supported by a single comparison (Gemma-2-2B vs. Gemma-2-9B, one layer pair each) plus the Llama-3.1-8B/70B case study. Two data points per claim is insufficient to establish a scale trend, and the 2B result is actually weaker than RePS, so the trend is not monotonic.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Evaluate on a wider range of model sizes (e.g., 1B/2B/7B/9B/13B/70B) at matched layers, or at minimum add a third size, and report whether the improvement with scale is statistically significant rather than anecdotal.

key_concerns.issue: Baselines in the case studies are cherry-picked: BiPO is excluded for 'consistent suboptimal performance on AXBENCH,' but excluding a baseline because it is weak is not a fair comparison. The case-study baseline set (DIM, RePS, DAS) is small and DAS is the authors' own ablation, leaving only two independent strong baselines.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Include BiPO (and ideally RePS variants) in both case studies for a fair, complete comparison. Justify baseline selection on principled grounds (representativeness) rather than performance.

key_concerns.issue: The title and abstract overclaim 'faithful bi-directional' steering, but CDAS fails on Phi-3.5-mini for refusal suppression (Table 2: only 30% suppression vs. RePS 68%) and DAS (the Lang.+DII variant) does worse than DIM on refusal. The 'faithful' and 'bi-directional' properties are not uniformly achieved.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Scope the title and abstract to the evidence: e.g., 'Distribution-Matching Steering with Distributed Interchange Interventions.' State explicitly in the abstract where CDAS fails (small models, certain layers) rather than only where it succeeds.

key_concerns.issue: Case study 2 (backdoor) is narrow: a single model (Llama-3.1-8B), 3 seeds, tinyBenchmarks of only 100 instances, and ASR that varies sharply by layer (e.g., CDAS@L16 6.68% on trigger but other layers much higher). The claim of 'effective override' rests on a single best layer selected post-hoc.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Add at least one more backdoored model or trigger type, report ASR across all tested layers with variance, and avoid selecting the best layer post-hoc for the headline result.

key_concerns.issue: The faithfulness argument is partly circular: CDAS is trained to minimize JSD (closely related to KL), and then evaluated for faithfulness via KL divergence. Low KL is expected by construction and does not independently establish that steering is 'causally grounded' or concept-faithful.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Add an independent faithfulness measure not optimized during training (e.g., causal scrubbing, interchange intervention accuracy on held-out counterfactuals, or probing-based concept localization agreement) to substantiate the 'causally grounded' claim.

key_concerns.issue: No analysis of why CDAS fails on Phi-3.5-mini or why DAS (Lang.+DII) underperforms DIM on refusal. The paper asserts CDAS 'may benefit from scale' but offers no mechanistic explanation, weakening the interpretability framing that motivates the method.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Provide diagnostic experiments (e.g., feature geometry, subspace overlap with known refusal directions, effect of model architecture) that explain the failure cases and the scale trend.

questions_for_authors: Given that unit-factor CDAS scores 0.12–0.24 on AXBENCH (Table 1), how can the 'faithful, tuning-free' framing in the title and abstract be justified? What is the principled reason the unit factor underperforms, and is it a bug or a fundamental limitation?

Tables 1–4 report single numbers. What is the variance across seeds, and do the claimed advantages (e.g., 0.023 layer-consistency gap, KL superiority) remain statistically significant once variance is reported?
On what principled grounds is BiPO excluded from the case studies? Could you report BiPO results to confirm it is indeed not a competitive baseline in these settings?
The 'scale benefit' claim rests on 2B vs. 9B (AXBENCH) and 8B vs. 70B (refusal). Would the trend hold on a third size (e.g., 13B)?

Since CDAS is trained with JSD and evaluated for faithfulness with KL (a closely related divergence), how do you rule out that low KL is not simply an artifact of the training objective? Can you provide an independent faithfulness measure?
Why does CDAS fail to suppress refusal on Phi-3.5-mini (30% vs. RePS 68%)? Is this a data, architecture, or scale issue?
calibration_check: Claims are partially over-scoped: the title and abstract assert 'faithful bi-directional' steering as a general property, but the body shows CDAS fails on small models, requires factor tuning on AXBENCH, and the 'scale benefit' rests on two data points—claims should be narrowed to the configurations and model sizes where evidence actually supports them.

significance.justification: The perspective shift (steering as causal concept identification) is interesting and the safety case studies are practical, but CDAS does not clearly advance steering effectiveness over RePS and its principled advantage (faithfulness) is not empirically established, limiting likely impact.

novelty.justification: The combination of a JSD distribution-matching objective with DII for bi-directional steering is genuinely new relative to Lang./PO steering methods, though each component (DII, distribution matching) exists in prior work.

rigor.justification: Method is sound in principle but the claim–evidence link is weak: the principled configuration underperforms, scale claims rest on one comparison, and failure cases lack diagnostic analysis.

statistical_soundness.justification: No error bars, variance, or significance tests in any of the four main tables; Figure 1 uses only 3 seeds; key claims (consistency, scale benefit) are based on single-run numbers and are not statistically supported.

calibration_honesty.justification: The conclusion honestly lists limitations, but the title/abstract overclaim 'faithful bi-directional' steering despite unit-factor failure and small-model failures; claims about scale benefits and causal grounding exceed the evidence.

clarity.justification: The method is mostly well explained with clear preliminaries and intuition, but the objective derivation is dense and the relationship between CDAS and DAS (and why DAS underperforms) is not clearly articulated.

structure_compliance.justification: Standard Abstract/Introduction/Related Work/Method/Experiments/Conclusion structure is followed and the paper is within reasonable conference length; organization of case studies is logical.

reproducibility.justification: Method, hyperparameters, and data curation are described at a level that would permit reproduction if appendix links were restored; however, grid-search ranges and exact token-position selection details are under-specified in the main text.

related_work.justification: Prior work on steering, causal variable localization, distribution matching, and safety mechanisms is covered fairly, though the delineation between CDAS and DAS as a steering method vs. a localization method could be sharper.

figure_quality.justification: Captions describe informative comparisons (ASR by layer, KL divergence, benchmark preservation), but tables lack variance and the single figure reports only 3 seeds; display items support but do not strongly strengthen the claims.

breadth_generality.justification: AXBENCH covers many concepts but only two model sizes; case studies use few models, cherry-picked baselines, and tinyBenchmarks of 100 instances—generality is under-supported relative to the broad claims made.

overall_recommendation.justification: A promising and novel perspective with useful safety case studies, but the principled configuration underperforms, statistics are absent, baselines are cherry-picked, and the title overclaims; substantial added experiments and rescoping are needed to reach the ICLR bar.
